title: Holographic and Immersive Theatre
desc: Plan an immersive or holographic show: concept, stage tech, safety, rights, budget and audience care.
outcomes: Explain holographic effects and immersive formats.
task: Produce a production plan for a short immersive or hologram-style show, with concept, tech list, safety plan, access plan, budget and run sheet.
condition: A computer, a spreadsheet, a venue plan, two peers and a mentor. No live public show is run by learners.
standard: Effects are described accurately (illusion methods named); safety and fire plans approved; access plan included; budget totals correct; peers rate Meets or better.
who: Stage managers, event planners, students, museum staff.
evidence: concept, tech list, safety plan, budget, run sheet
modules: Formats: how holograms and immersive shows are really made
Understand
Many shows called holographic use clever illusions rather than true 3D light. Knowing the methods helps you choose well and describe the show honestly.
Reflected-image effects use an angled clear screen to make a figure appear to float on stage.
Projection mapping paints images onto buildings, sets or objects.
Walk-through immersive rooms combine projection, sound, scent and movement.
Headset VR and augmented reality add personal 3D views.

A reflected-image effect uses a bright screen below an angled transparent sheet. The audience sees a figure floating while the sheet is almost invisible in a dark room. A visit to a local exhibit shows how a hidden screen creates depth.
Compare three formats in a table with how it works, cost, room needs and best use.
Build an accurate table that names the illusion method.
Story, audience and guest flow
Create
Technology serves the story. Start with who the show is for and what they should feel.
Write one idea, one audience and one feeling.
Map the journey in scenes with time and mood.
Plan the first minute carefully; it sets the rules.
Plan how guests move from entry to exit with one-way routes to avoid crowding.
A museum plans a six-scene walk about local rivers: arrival, spring, flood, drought, repair, hope. Each scene lasts four minutes and uses one main effect.
Write a one-page concept, a six-scene map and a flow map.
State audience, feeling, scene times and guest flow in the concept.
Stage technology and backups
Apply
Lighting, projection and sound must work together.
Projector brightness is measured in lumens; a small dark room needs about 3,000 to 5,000; large rooms need more.
Throw distance and screen size set image size and clarity.
Control room, cue lists and spare equipment.
Sound design and timing with visuals.
A 5,000-lumen projector with a 1.5 throw ratio at 4.5 m gives a 3 m wide image, enough for a small dark room. A spare projector is mounted ready.
List equipment, cables, power and spares for your show.
List specs and spares.
Safety in the dark
Evaluate
People move in low light and may be startled.
Exits lit and clear; capacity from exit width.
Trip hazards removed or marked; handrails for steps.
Warnings for flashing lights and loud sounds.
Trained staff, an emergency plan and a rehearsal of turning on the house lights.
Capacity is limited to 150 from exit width, following the venue's and local authority's rules, and a fire plan is approved by the venue. Staff practise turning on the house lights.
Write a safety plan.
Plan is approved by the venue.
Access and inclusion
Evaluate
Everyone should be able to enjoy the show.
Step-free routes, seating, captions and audio description.
Low-sensory sessions with softer sound and steady light.
Clear signs and a quiet area.
Ask a disabled guest to test the route.
A quiet hour with lower sound and steady lights lets sensory-sensitive guests attend. A wheelchair user finds a threshold too high and a ramp is added.
Write an access plan and a tester feedback form.
List the measures and test them.
Rights, permissions and content
Apply
Clear everything before show day.
Music, images, scripts and performers need permission.
Written agreements and credits.
Performer consent for filming.
Keep contracts and licences in a binder.
A performer consent form covers filming and archive use and is signed before rehearsal. A music licence is filed before opening night.
Complete a rights sheet and binder list.
Give a source for all items.
Budget and break-even
Analyse
Plan the money.
Equipment hire, crew, venue, marketing and a contingency of about 10 per cent.
Ticket price x seats x shows.
Break-even audience.
Test low sales.
Costs of 200,000 INR with a 400 INR ticket (estimates; check your market) gives break-even at 500 tickets across 4 shows, or 125 per show. A 20,000 INR contingency is held.
Build a budget with break-even and a low-sales case.
Show the currency and calculate totals correctly.
Run sheet and rehearsal
Create
Run smoothly.
Cue sheet and roles.
Technical and dress rehearsals.
Rehearse a failure of each system, such as a power cut.
Debrief and fix.
A rehearsal finds a cue 3 seconds late and the cue sheet is corrected. The team practises a power cut and restores the show in two minutes.
Write a run sheet and practise one failure.
Run sheet is complete and the failure drill is logged.
quiz: How are many stage holograms made?
Images show brighter and the hidden sheet stays unseen.
rubric: Each effect has its hazard (light, laser, haze, crowd) noted
Hazards rehearsed once and the notes show what changed
Capacity, fire exit, haze and access rules for the place are written down
Rules checked with the venue and authority and an exit drill timed

local: Public safety and licensing rules differ by place.
